name: Workload Modernization Agent
description: Decides what should happen to each workload running on a virtual machine: become a container, or stay a virtual machine. Reads what is actually running inside each guest through VMware Tools — guest OS, power state and the process list with command lines — scores it against the things that make a container the wrong answer, and reports the candidate rate against the whole estate as well as against the machines that answered. Refuses to score a machine it could not read: an unread machine is reported as unread, never as having no blockers. The disposition it can reach that a containerisation tool cannot is “keep this as a virtual machine”, with the reason.
capabilities: Read guest OS, hostname, addresses and VMware Tools state for a whole wave using the credential MTV already holds — no agent, nothing installed
Read the running process list and command lines through VMware Tools guest operations, which executes nothing inside the guest and writes nothing to it
Recognise the application runtime from its command line — Tomcat, JBoss, WebLogic, WebSphere, Spring Boot, .NET, Node.js, Python, PHP, Ruby, nginx, httpd — and suggest a UBI base image for each
Treat an application server as subsuming what runs inside it, so a Spring application on Tomcat is one workload rather than three
Block on a local datastore and say the data is the reason: PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Cassandra, Db2 or Kafka running on the machine
Block on a desktop session, OS-level clustering, a node-locked licence daemon, nested virtualisation, or a machine that is already a container host
Report a Windows guest as needing its own node pool through the Windows Machine Config Operator, rather than dismissing it
Flag multi-application hosts and directory-joined machines as work to resolve before anything is built
Report backup, monitoring, security and configuration-management agents as things that will not come with the workload, without blocking on them
Name every fact that could not be read — listening ports, unit files, packages, scheduled jobs, kernel modules, config — and cap confidence because of them
Distinguish a machine that answered with no processes from one that could not be read at all
Tell apart the four reasons guest operations fail: a rejected guest credential, VMware Tools not answering, a missing vCenter privilege, and an unsupported guest
Report the candidate rate twice — against the whole estate and against the machines that answered — so a pilot is not sold on the second number
Propose a Containerfile per detected runtime on a UBI base — non-root, no systemd, an explicit USER, and a probe wired to the port
Propose the OpenShift manifests that would run it: Deployment with runAsNonRoot, a read-only root filesystem and all capabilities dropped, plus Service, Route and a default-deny NetworkPolicy
List every assumption behind the proposal separately from the findings — the port above all, which is a convention rather than a reading
Refuse to generate anything for a machine that was blocked, powered off, unreadable or inconclusive, and say which of those it was
Refuse a licensed runtime such as WebLogic or WebSphere rather than inventing a base image for it

Hand code analysis to Red Hat MTA rather than reproducing it — discovers MTA across every API group it has shipped under (mta.konveyor.io, tackle.konveyor.io, konveyor.io), finds its Hub route, and reports a permissions problem as a permissions problem rather than as 'not installed'
Show MTA's findings beside the agent's own, each attributed to its source and never blended into one score: MTA reports what is wrong inside the code, the agent what is wrong around it on the machine
Carry MTA's effort estimate in its own story points, multiplied by incidents rather than by rules, and exclude unestimated findings from the total instead of scoring them zero
Propose the build on tooling the customer already owns: an OpenShift ImageStream and a BuildConfig carrying the reviewed Containerfile inline, so what was read is what gets built
Propose a binary build that needs no git repository, because an application on a twelve-year-old VM very often is not in one
Propose a Tekton pipeline using the Buildah, git-clone and openshift-client ClusterTasks that ship with OpenShift Pipelines, leaving the image scanner unpinned for the customer to choose
boundaries: Read-only. Builds no image, writes nothing to any guest, creates nothing on the target cluster.
Executes no command inside a guest. Listening ports, systemd units, installed packages and configuration files are therefore reported as unread rather than as absent.
Never returns high confidence, because the facts that would justify it cannot be read without executing something in the guest.
Guest credentials are supplied per call and never persisted.
Scores no machine it could not read, and counts no unread machine as a candidate.
Proposes only. Builds no image, tags nothing, pushes nothing, deploys nothing.
Cannot extract the application's files, because it executes nothing in the guest — the Containerfile is a scaffold with placeholder COPY paths, and says so in its own header.
Sets no CPU or memory requests. A VM's shape is not a container's requirement, and copying one to the other is the most expensive mistake available here.
Submits no artefact to MTA. MTA analyses a war, jar or repository; this agent executes nothing in a guest and cannot extract one, so a human or a pipeline supplies it.
Starts no build and runs no pipeline. Every manifest is proposed for a human to apply.
